heaps/01_heapify_by_hand: Heapify turns a plain list into a min-heap in place, the move when you have all the numbers up front. Children of index i sit at 2i+1 and 2i+2, so the last parent is n//2 - 1; walk from there down to 0 and sift each node toward its smaller child. Every subtree below is already a heap, which is the invariant. People stop before the root or swap with the left child instead of the smaller one. Floyd's build is O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
heaps/02_push_and_pop_by_hand: This is the min-heap on a plain list you write when heapq is not allowed or you must explain it. Push appends the value and floats it up while it is smaller than its parent at (i-1)//2. Pop takes the root, moves the last element into slot 0, and sinks it toward the smaller child while that child is smaller. The classic slip is sinking toward the left child without comparing both children first. Each operation is O(log n) time, O(1) extra space.
heaps/03_top_k_with_size_k_min_heap: To find the k largest values in a list or a stream, keep a min-heap of size k instead of sorting everything. Its root is the smallest of the best so far, so it is the gatekeeper: a new value gets in only when it beats the root, and the root is what leaves. A min-heap finding the largest feels backwards at first. People push without checking the size, or pop then push instead of heappushpop. The cost is O(n log k) time and O(k) space.
heaps/04_max_heap_by_negation_and_tuples: Python's heapq is a min-heap only, so to pop the highest priority first you push the negated priority and flip the sign back on the way out. To carry a payload such as a dict, push the tuple (-priority, arrival, payload) where arrival is a counter bumped on every push. Equal priorities then fall back to arrival order, so ties pop first in, first out and Python never compares two payloads. Leaving out the counter crashes when two equal priorities carry uncomparable payloads. Each push and pop is O(log n).
heaps/06_merge_k_sorted_arrays: Merging k sorted arrays into one sorted output calls for a min-heap holding one candidate per array, keyed as (value, which array, position). Pop the smallest, append it, and push the successor from the same array. The invariant is that the heap always holds the smallest unseen element of every array, so pops come out in global sorted order. People forget to skip empty arrays when seeding, or push past the end of an array. With N elements in total it is O(N log k) time, O(k) space.
tries/02_trie_delete: Deleting a word from a trie is more than clearing a flag: nodes no other word needs should be pruned. Walk down recording the path, clear the end flag at the last node, then unwind toward the root, deleting a child only while it has no children and does not end another word. At the first shared node, stop. People prune on the way down, or delete nodes that still end a shorter word like app inside apple. The cost is O(length of the word) in time and path space.
tries/03_autocomplete_collect_words_with: Autocomplete asks for every stored word that starts with a prefix, and a trie answers in two steps. First walk the prefix character by character; if the path breaks, return an empty list. Then depth-first search below that node, visiting children in alphabetical order so the words come out sorted for free, emitting a word at every end flag. The usual mistake is starting the DFS with an empty string instead of the prefix already spelled. The walk is O(prefix length); the DFS costs the size of the matching subtree.
backtracking/02_subsets_with_duplicates: Subsets with duplicates is the start-index subset template plus one skip rule. Sort first so equal values sit side by side. At every level record the path, extend it with each value from the start index onward, and recurse from i + 1. Skip a value equal to its left neighbor unless i is this level's start, so a run of equals is chosen once per level. People forget to sort, or write i > 0 instead of i > start. Cost is O(n times 2 to the n).
backtracking/03_combinations_n_choose_k: Combinations picks k numbers from 1 to n where order does not matter, so each choice recurses from i + 1 to keep results increasing and avoid repeats. The path grows one number at a time; when it reaches length k, copy it into the results and return. Break the loop early once the numbers left cannot fill the open slots. People forget the copy and append the same mutable list, or recurse from i and reuse a number. Time is O(k times C(n, k)), space O(k) for the path.
backtracking/06_permutations_with_duplic: Permutations with duplicates uses a used[] array of flags, since every value is placed somewhere, plus sorting and one skip rule so identical orderings never appear twice. Among a run of equal values the recursion must take them left to right, so skip nums[i] when it equals nums[i - 1] and that left twin is not yet used. Writing used[i - 1] instead of not used[i - 1] is the common flip. Remember to unmark the flag as well as popping the path. The cost is O(n times n factorial).
bits/01_get_set_clear_toggle_bits: Every single-bit operation starts with the mask 1 << i, a lone 1 at position i counting from the right, zero-based. OR with the mask forces that bit to 1, AND with the complement ~mask forces it to 0, XOR flips it, and shifting n right by i then AND 1 reads it. Writing a value v into bit i is clear first, then OR in v << i; people skip the clear and an old 1 survives when v is 0. Every operation is O(1).
bits/02_count_bits_and_lowest_set_bit: Two identities do most bit-counting work. Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit to 0 and every 0 below it to 1, so n & (n - 1) clears exactly that bit; loop until n is 0 to count the set bits, Kernighan's trick. Likewise n & -n keeps only the lowest set bit. A positive number is a power of two exactly when dropping its lowest set bit leaves 0; forgetting the n > 0 guard lets 0 through. Everything here is O(1) or O(set bits).
bits/03_xor_tricks_single_number_missing: XOR cancels pairs because x ^ x is 0 and x ^ 0 is x, so XOR-ing a whole list leaves whatever appeared an odd number of times. Single number is just that fold. Missing number XORs every index and every value so each present value cancels its own index; people forget to start the accumulator at n. For two singles, XOR everything, take the lowest set bit of the result, and XOR only the elements having that bit. All three are O(n) time, O(1) space.
bits/04_bitmask_subset_enumeration: A subset of n items is an n-bit integer where bit i set means items[i] is in, so counting masks from 0 up to 2 to the n visits every subset once without recursion. To list only the subsets of a given mask, start at the mask and repeat sub = (sub - 1) & mask: the borrow stays inside the mask's bits, so each step lands on the next smaller submask. People forget to record 0 after the loop ends. All subsets cost O(2 to the n times n).
bits/05_reverse_bits_and_shifts: Reversing the 32 bits of an unsigned integer is a peel-and-push loop: take the lowest bit with n & 1, shift the result left and OR that bit in, then shift n right. Run exactly 32 rounds even after n reaches 0, because the input's leading zeros must become the output's trailing zeros; stopping early is the classic bug. Also, Python's >> keeps the sign, so -8 >> 1 is -4; a logical 32-bit shift masks with 0xFFFFFFFF first. Both are O(32), effectively constant time and space.
math/01_gcd_lcm_euclid: Euclid finds the greatest common divisor by replacing the pair (a, b) with (b, a % b) until b is 0; then a is the answer. It works because every common divisor of a and b also divides a % b, so the gcd never changes while the numbers shrink fast. The least common multiple is the product divided by the gcd; divide before multiplying so the intermediate stays small. People stop when the remainder reaches 1 instead of 0. Time is O(log of the smaller number), space O(1).
math/02_primes_sieve_and_primality: Trial division tests one number: no d up to its square root divides it, since a factor above the root pairs with one below. The sieve lists every prime up to n: mark 2 to n as prime, then for each surviving p with p squared at most n cross off p squared and every p-th number after it. People write d * d < n instead of <= and miss perfect squares. Trial division is O(square root of n); the sieve is O(n log log n) time, O(n) space.
math/03_fast_power_and_modular_arithmeti: Fast power computes base to the exp by walking the bits of exp from the lowest: when the bit is 1, multiply the current base into the result; then square the base and shift exp right. Each squaring doubles the power the base stands for, so 13 as 1101 in binary becomes 3 times 81 times 6561. For modular exponentiation reduce every product mod m, which keeps numbers small. People start the result at base instead of 1, giving one factor too many. The loop is O(log exp), O(1) space.
math/04_digits_reverse_integer_and_palin: Digit problems peel the lowest digit with n % 10, drop it with n // 10, and rebuild with rev = rev * 10 + digit so the lowest digit becomes the highest. Reverse integer does this on the absolute value, restores the sign, and returns 0 outside the signed 32-bit range, a check Python will not do for you. Palindrome number reverses only the lower half of the digits and compares it with the rest. People forget that a trailing zero rules out a palindrome. Both are O(digits).
math/05_base_conversion_and_excel_column: Base conversion is repeated division: n % b gives the lowest digit, n // b drops it, and the digits come out lowest first, so reverse at the end. Reading back is Horner's rule, n = n * b + digit. Excel columns are base 26 with A through Z standing for 1 through 26 and no zero, so subtract 1 before dividing; otherwise 26 comes out as BA instead of Z. That missing minus one is what everybody gets wrong. Both directions cost O(digits).
math/06_random_pick_and_reservoir_sampli: Reservoir sampling picks k items uniformly from a stream whose length you do not know, in one pass and O(k) memory. Fill the reservoir with the first k items, then let item i replace a random slot j = randrange(i + 1) only when j is less than k; every item is kept with probability k over n. With k equal to 1 over the indices holding a target value, this is Random Pick Index. People call randrange(i) instead of randrange(i + 1), which skews the odds. Time is O(n).
matrices/04_search_2d_matrix_staircase: When every row and every column of a matrix is sorted, search it by walking a staircase from the top-right corner. If the cell is bigger than the target, everything below it is bigger too, so move left and drop the column; if smaller, everything to its left is smaller, so move down and drop the row. One comparison always rules out an entire line, which is why the corner matters. People start at the top-left, where nothing can be discarded. The walk is O(m + n) time, O(1) space.
matrices/05_game_of_life_in_place: Game of Life: a live cell with 2 or 3 live neighbors survives, a dead cell with exactly 3 comes alive, everything else dies, and every cell must read its neighbors' old state. To update in place, pack two bits per cell: bit 0 holds the current state, bit 1 receives the next, and a final pass shifts every cell right by one. Count neighbors with & 1 so updated cells do not leak. People let 2 neighbors revive a dead cell. O(m times n) time, O(1) extra space.
matrices/06_matrix_traversal_patterns: Most grid problems begin with walking the cells and finding a cell's neighbors. Row-major goes row by row, column-major column by column, and anti-diagonals group cells by row plus col, giving m + n - 1 diagonals clipped at the matrix edges. The direction vectors DIRS4 and DIRS8 plus a bounds check of 0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols produce the valid neighbors. The usual slip is writing <= on the upper bound. Every traversal is O(m times n).
strings/02_two_pointer_palindromes_and_r: Two pointers on a string handle two common drills. For a palindrome check, start lo at the left end and hi at the right, step past anything that is not a letter or digit, and compare lowercase characters until the pointers cross. To reverse the words of a sentence in O(1) extra space, reverse the whole character list, then reverse each word back into reading order. The mistake is comparing case-sensitively, or moving both pointers at once. Both are O(n) time.
strings/03_kmp_prefix_function: KMP finds every occurrence of a pattern in a text in one pass. The failure table fail[i] stores the length of the longest proper prefix of the pattern up to i that is also its suffix, so on a mismatch after j matched characters the pattern slides to its longest border with j = fail[j - 1] instead of restarting. The fall-back is a while loop, not an if, because the next comparison may fail again. Time O(n + m), space O(m).
strings/04_rabin_karp_rolling_hash: Rabin-Karp compares a pattern against each window of the text by hash rather than by characters. The window hash is a polynomial in a base modulo a prime, and sliding one step costs O(1): subtract the leftmost character times its weight, multiply by the base, add the new character, reduce mod. Equal hashes are only a candidate, so confirm each hit with a direct string compare; skipping that check is the classic bug, because collisions happen. Expected time is O(n + m), worst case O(n times m), O(1) extra space.
strings/05_encode_decode_strings_and_joi: Encoding a list of strings into one string must survive any character. Write each piece as its length, a '#', then the text; the decoder reads digits up to the first '#', slices exactly that many characters, and jumps past them, so a '#' inside the payload never looks like a boundary. Collect the parts in a list and join once, because += in a loop recopies the accumulator and goes quadratic. People forget that an empty string encodes as '0#'. Both are O(total length).
